I get summonsed for almost every term for which I'm eligible. It's crazy how often I'm called. I have appeared in the pool at least 3 or 4 times, I've been through voir dire twice and didn't get picked either time. I suspect it may partly be due to the fact that I work in the legal field and know a lot of the people in Court already so I get conflicted out.

Also, just so you know, if you get summonsed for a jury, your background IS being investigated by the Plaintiffs/Prosecutors and Defendants. They get a list before trial of all the potential jurors. Smart counsel then will investigate your social media, your home ownership history, and anything else that can be found out about you online. It is all being dug up. You've been warned.
All I have under my real name is a dead facebook account (which is totally locked down to private) and anything which is professional and squeaky clean (Linkdin and other job sites mostly).

Called three times, picked twice, both times a plea deal was reached before opening statements. First time was a low level drug dealer, second was child porn related and the one I wasn't picked for was a DUI related death. It's been several years since the last time I got the postcard.

Never have, though If you ever want out of jury duty, raise your hand and ask "How does jury nullification work?" and voila! no more jury duty.

Though, if the case is something stupid like a suburban mom growing her own pot and facing felonies for it I would most definitely try to stay on the jury list and push for NG.
Ding, ding, ding! Exactly! I've never been called up but when people I know are, I tell them this. Great legal way to get out of it if you don't want to do it.
followed the news on my trial through the whole case - cuz wtf they expect me ocd todo. spilled the mother fucking beans on a few beaners. case tossed.

This one woman really wanted to be jury forewoman, told every about her college degree in communications. No one else wanted the job. I made her cry when she could not define the word 'imminent'.

This one jackass, in jury selection, said he is against capital punishment, turned out he is against any punishment.

I thought the deliberation would be an hour or less, the case was simple. We were there for five days. We had a verdict of manslaughter instead of murder. The defendant is a murderer but I had to go along with manslaughter or risk a hung jury.

Been on two (one of those I was an alternate, which means I was there for everything but deliberations). Both were civil cases.

One was a worker suing the state highway agency for a injury during road construction. Pretty nasty, he basically lost half his foot. But we found for the defense, because there just wasn't enough evidence that the highway agency was to blame for the accident. I presume he already got worker's comp and couldn't sue his direct employer for that reason. But alot of jurors were very emotionally swayed by his ordeal. So it was a fairly close split, 7 to 5 or something like that. In a civil case it doesn't have to be unanimous.

The other was about a car accident. And the defendant admitted they ran a red light. Pretty open-and-shut in terms of fault, so the trial was really all about damages. The plaintiff claimed he suffered debilitating back pain, needed surgery and probably more in the future, etc. Frankly I'm glad I didn't have to decide that one, it's almost impossible to know if or how much he was telling the truth. But I did stick around for the verdict, they gave him significantly less than he asked for, but still a nice chunk of money.

I think trials should determine verdict and penalty/damages in separate phases. And the first part should be strictly policed for lawyers trying to emotionally sway the jury.
